# R

## R -- Software for statistical computing

<br>

**R** can be downloaded [here](https://www.r-project.org): <https://www.r-project.org/>

<br>

You can use the graphical user interface that comes with **R**, or you
can run **R** through a system like **ESS+emacs** or **RStudio**
(<https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>)\

<br>

Most people use **RStudio** these days


## RStudio

![](figs/rstudio-no-script.PNG){.framed-img fig-align="center" width="90%"}

To create a new script, click: `File > New File > R Script`

Save your script using: `File > Save As`

## Reproducing the Excel exercise 

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

Create an object called [`year`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"}
to hold the sequence of years.^[Everything in the boxes is R code that you can copy and paste into your script in RStudio. Everything below the boxes is R output.]

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: year
year <- 1950:1961 # A vector of integers
year              # Type the name of an object to see its values
```

::: {.fragment}
Note that you can use [`seq`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} to
create sequences in a more general way. The [`c`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} function combines two or more vectors.

```{r} 
#| echo: true
#| label: seq
updown <- c(seq(from=20, to=100, by=20), seq(from=100, to=20, by=-20))
updown            # Two sequences, combined
```
:::


::: {.fragment}
Use the `length` function to determine the number of values in a
vector.


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: nYears
nYears <- length(year)
nYears
```
:::

:::



## A simple population model

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}

Create an empty vector to store the data on females. Set female
abundance to 100 in the first year.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: females
females <- rep(NA, nYears)
females[1] <- 100
```

<br>

::: {.fragment}
Use a "for loop" to compute female abundance in subsequent years.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: femaleLoop
for(t in 2:nYears) {
    females[t] <- females[t-1] + females[t-1]*0.01
}
```

:::

<br>

<center>
::: {.fragment}
[**We will use "for loops" for almost every population model that we
implement in R**]{.alert}
:::
</center>

:::

## A simple population model

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='40%'}
Generate the data on males using a single line of code.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: males
males <- females*0.8
```
:::

::: {.column width="5%"}
:::


::: {.column width='55%' .fragment}
Put the objects in a `data.frame`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: data
model1 <- data.frame(year, females, males)
model1
```
:::
:::

:::


## Graphics



```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
plot(females ~ year, data=model1, type="o", xlab="Year", ylab="Abundance",
     lwd=2, pch=16, ylim=c(0, 120))
lines(males ~ year, data=model1, type="o", col="blue", lwd=2, pch=16)
legend(x=1950, y=40, legend=c("Females", "Males"), col=c("black", "blue"),
       lty=1, pch=16)
```


## Graphics

::: {style="font-size: 75%"}

Another way to do the same thing, without putting objects in a `data.frame`:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: plot-v2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
plot(x=year, y=females, type="o", xlab="Year", ylab="Abundance",
     lwd=2, pch=16, ylim=c(0, 120))
lines(x=year, y=males, type="o", col="blue", lwd=2, pch=16)
legend(x=1950, y=40, legend=c("Females", "Males"), col=c("black", "blue"), lty=1, pch=16)
```

:::



## Assignment

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}

1.  Create an Excel file and name it "Yourlastname_Yourfirstname".

2.  Create the sheet shown on the next page using the techniques covered
    in this lab.

    - Use auto-fill to create the first two columns.

    - For the "Adults" column, use the equation shown for cells C3
      through C22. Note: For cell C2, you can directly enter the value
      "10".

3.  Copy "Sheet1" to a new sheet and change the color and thickness of
    the lines. You can pick any colors and thicknesses you want.

4.  Replicate steps 1--3 using a "for loop" in a self-contained R
    script. Note that you will need code to create both graphs---the
    original one and the one with the new line color and thickness.

    - Hint: You can make the juveniles data using `seq` and `c`, like
      we did with the `updown` example earlier.

5.  Upload the Excel workbook (with both sheets) and the R script to ELC
    by 5:00pm on Friday.^[Always clear your RStudio workspace and
    rerun the R script before uploading to ELC.]

:::
